cues.text: Midnight Mass at a Marian Shrine

On the night of December 8, 1991, the Feast of the Immaculate Conception, Father Otty Ossa Aristizabal, chaplain of the Marian shrine of Finca Betania in Cua, Venezuela, celebrated midnight Mass before a large gathering of pilgrims.
Following the consecration, he divided the large Host into four parts as was his custom before Communion.
Father Otty consumed one of the four pieces and set the remaining three aside on the paten — and noticed that one of them had begun to bleed.
Not wishing to cause alarm among the assembled pilgrims, he said nothing at the time, and after Mass placed the bleeding fragment in the tabernacle overnight.
The following day, Father Otty found the Host still bleeding, the blood flowing from only one side without staining the rest of the fragment.
He and those present took care to confirm the blood had not come from the priest himself.
They then showed the Host to pilgrims who had gathered for morning Mass before reporting the matter to his bishop, the Most Reverend Pio Bello Ricardo.
Bishop Bello Ricardo had the Host tested at a hospital in Caracas, where the substance was determined to be human blood; he subsequently approved the authenticity of the event.

The Host is preserved today at the convent of the Augustinian Recollect Sisters of the Sacred Heart of Jesus in Los Teques, permanently exposed for the adoration of pilgrims who continue to visit from within Venezuela and abroad.

Betania was already a recognized site of Marian devotion by 1991, its apparitions to Maria Esperanza approved by the Church some years earlier, giving the Eucharistic sign a devotional context already familiar to those who came to witness it.

The shrine's dual identity — a place of Marian apparition and, separately, a formally approved Eucharistic sign — has drawn pilgrims to Betania and its Los Teques convent for more than three decades since.
